In this study, FMT from ICI responders was used to assess if gut microbiota modulation could overcome established ICI resistance in different cancer types. All patients had progressed on ICIs in the metastatic setting. We found that the study interventions had an acceptable safety profile, and that FMT was feasible in patients with advanced cancer, but observed no objective responses. A patient with melanoma had clinical benefit as defined in the protocol, with stable disease lasting more than 6 months, and remains alive after 33 months. Another patient with melanoma, who had no prior response or toxicity to ICIs, developed both evidence of response and immune-related toxicity, but eventually progressed and died. There has to our knowledge been no previous reports on FMT in HNSCC. In our trial, the patient with HNSCC had stable disease for 20 weeks and remains alive after 16 months. The potential risk of transmission of infectious agents is a concern with FMT.^{31} However, FMT has for decades been used for Clostridioides difficile infections, and the available data indicate that most FMT-related AEs are low-grade and self-limiting.^{32} Previous trials have indicated that FMT is safe also in patients with cancer,18,2033 and the results from our trial, MITRIC, support the safety of FMT in patients with advanced cancer. All AEs related to FMT treatment were grade 1, while one grade 3 event was recorded following colonoscopy. IrAEs occurred in 50% of patients and were mostly mild. Five out of six patients with irAEs in MITRIC had also experienced irAEs prior to study enrollment, suggesting that FMT did not increase the risk of irAEs. We furthermore found that irAEs were related to higher baseline PBMC levels of differentiated CD4+T cells with an EM and Th1 phenotype, as well as Tregs and ICOS^{+} CD8 T cells. This observation suggests that a pre-existing activated immune milieu may predispose to irAEs. However, from our dataset, it cannot be determined whether this phenotype was induced by prior ICI exposure. Previous single-arm studies have reported a potential for FMT to reverse ICI resistance. Two proof-of-concept trials in metastatic melanoma demonstrated clinical benefit in patients with anti-PD-1-refractory disease: Baruch et al^{19} reported objective responses in 3 of 10 patients, and Davar et al^{18} reported responses in 3 of 15 patients, with durable stable disease in three additional patients. Kim et al^{20} observed objective responses in 1 of 13 patients with upper gastrointestinal cancers progressing on PD-1 inhibition. FMT combined with ICIs is also being evaluated in the first-line setting. Recently, several single-arm studies have evaluated healthy-donor FMT in combination with anti-PD-1 monotherapy or anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4 therapy as first-line treatment in advanced melanoma,^{36 37} advanced non-small cell lung cancer^{36} and metastatic RCC.^{34} These studies suggest that FMT may enhance the efficacy of ICIs in the treatment-naïve setting. In addition, results from the randomized TACITO trial were recently published,^{35} indicating potential clinical activity of FMT combined with first-line anti-PD-1 therapy and a tyrosine kinase inhibitor in metastatic RCC, using ICI responders as donors. Various factors may explain the discrepancy between encouraging findings from previous FMT studies and the absence of confirmed responses in MITRIC. First, the small sample size represents an important limitation, as in earlier FMT trials conducted in ICI-resistant disease. Second, heterogeneity across studies—including differences in donor selection, FMT preparation, route of administration, and treatment schedule—may influence clinical and biological outcomes. Patient selection is also likely critical. In the studies by Baruch et al, Davar et al, and Kim et al, most responses occurred relatively late and were sometimes preceded by pseudo-progression, suggesting that patients with rapidly progressive disease and short expected survival may not be optimal candidates.18,20 In MITRIC, most patients presented with disseminated, fast-growing disease, which may not have allowed sufficient time for FMT to exert meaningful effects. We included both patients with and without previous ICI benefit, and it remains unclear in which clinical context microbiota modulation is most relevant. The recently accumulating first-line evidence,^{34 36 37} including randomized data,^{35} raises the possibility that the ICI-naïve setting may be better suited for FMT strategies. Donor characteristics are also likely crucial. As in other trials of ICI-refractory disease, we used long-term ICI responders as stool donors; however, microbial composition varies considerably among such donors, and it is unknown whether this approach is superior to using healthy donors. The small number of available donors adds uncertainty. Notably, all responders in Baruch et al received stool from a single donor,^{19} whereas our study used three donors, raising the possibility of suboptimal donor-recipient matching or lack of specific microbial communities required for benefit. Donor age may also influence microbial diversity, although older donors were likewise used in Davar et al.^{18} Finally, microbiota composition is shaped by diet, geography, medications, and host factors, contributing to inconsistent “beneficial” signatures across studies.^{13 14} Thus, FMT may be effective only in selected populations, and the gut microbiota represents just one of several determinants of immunotherapy outcome; reliable biomarkers to identify patients most likely to benefit from microbiota modulation have not yet been established. The MITRIC trial used repeated FMT treatments, under the premise that this should increase engraftment and thus the possibility of clinical success. The gut microbiota in most recipients shifted towards their respective donors 1 week after the first FMT, but this effect seemed transient in most recipients. As the patients progressed, it was not feasible to collect stool samples at later time points to assess long-term engraftment and the effects of repeated FMTs. One patient had long-term engraftment and, intriguingly, this was the only patient with clinical benefit in the study. This is in line with FMT studies in melanoma that have suggested long-term donor-recipient similarities only in responders.^{33} The PBMC data suggest that in this patient population, a highly differentiated T-cell environment is associated with improved PFS and OS, while a myeloid skewed and Th2-like environment suggests a poor prognosis. These findings are in line with existing knowledge on cancer immunity,^{4 38} and may reflect that these patients are treated with ICIs, which relies on the host immune response for their efficacy. The OS times calculated from the start of ICI therapy support that these observations represent immunological characteristics prognostic for patients treated with ICIs, and are not related to the FMT intervention. In particular, granzyme B^{+} CD8^{+} T cells were associated with favorable outcomes. Using the same mass cytometry panel, we recently identified this particular subset to be associated with clinical benefit from ICIs in a randomized breast cancer study.^{26} The FMT in MITRIC did not appear to induce changes in the systemic immune milieu, as measured by peripheral PBMC phenotypes. It would be of interest to explore if other FMT protocols or microbiota interventions could alter the PBMC signatures, and if this is related to clinical efficacy from FMT. Davar et al found that the clinical responders exhibited higher levels of CD56+CD8+ T cells in PBMCs after FMT/anti-PD-1 treatment, and that this subset expressed higher levels of various activation markers.^{18} Furthermore, Davar et al reported that responding patients had decreased circulating IL-8 and decreased frequencies of IL-8-producing myeloid cells in tumors. In contrast, we observed an increase in CD14^{+} monocytes and IL-8 during the study. Moreover, higher CD14^{+} monocyte levels after 4 weeks were in MITRIC associated with shorter PFS and OS. It is possible that increasing myeloid-driven immunosuppression in our patients during the course of the trial was related to the lack of benefit from FMT. However, the exploratory PBMC and cytokine data were not corrected for multiple testing in this study, and these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size. In conclusion, the MITRIC trial demonstrated that FMT in combination with ICIs is safe and feasible in patients with advanced cancers. While indications of clinical activity were observed in a few patients, FMT did not result in objective clinical responses in patients refractory to ICIs. Further research is needed to clarify whether FMT can enhance ICI efficacy, optimize FMT protocols, and establish criteria for donor and recipient selection. title: Safety and efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation in solid cancers resistant to immune checkpoint inhibitors: results of the MITRIC trial
